blocks.html:
READING PASSAGE 1

You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 1–13, which are based on Reading Passage 1 below.

Advertising Needs Attention

The harder advertisers try to get your attention, the more your brain ignores them.

Jane Raymond, a consumer psychologist at the University of Wales in Bangor, is carefully holding and gazing at a bottle of Chillz mineral water like a baby. Despite being made of clear plastic, it looks as if it has been carved from ice. This simple feature means shoppers are drawn to this bottle over the others on the shelf and cannot resist picking it up, Raymond says. She studies the subtle factors that motivate us to buy what we buy and advises big companies on how powerful an advertisement is and how it could be designed to stick more firmly in a consumer's memory. Most of all, she works out how to attract your attention.

In today's fast-paced consumer world, attention is in short supply. Whether we are taking our time shopping in a mall, surfing the Internet for information, or just watching television as a form of passive entertainment, consumers are surrounded by messages—one every 15 seconds of our waking lives, according to some estimates. Last year, companies worldwide spent $401 billion on advertising, according to the independent World Advertising Research Centre in the UK. But as the graveyard of failed products shows, they usually get it wrong.

Nine out of ten new products meet an early death, says Jamie Rayner, director of research at ID Magasin, a UK consultancy specialising in consumer behaviour. And the reason, he explains, is simple: conventional advertising has ceased to work. Rayner and his colleagues have measured how consumers—particularly regular commuters—react to advertising, and their conclusion should alarm many executives. They used a camera embedded in a pair of glasses worn to and from work to record commuters' gaze as they glanced at advertisements on their journey. After analysing the recordings and questioning the subjects, they found that most of the advertisements made no impression at all: only about one per cent could be recalled without prompting. It seems that although we may be looking at brands and advertisements all day long, most of the time we're not taking anything in.

Raymond thinks she knows why. Her move from research in visual processing into consumer psychology began in the early 1990s, when she discovered some strange behaviours in the brain's attentional system. She showed people a stream of letters and numbers on a screen and asked them to look out for a letter X. When she asked her volunteers afterwards what they had seen, she found that if the X appeared up to half a second or so after the white letter, or vice versa, people failed to see it. She concluded that if something catches your attention, your brain is blind to anything else for a short period afterwards. She called this effect the "attentional blink.” “In short, the reason most advertising doesn't work is that we're in a severe state of attentional overload. Unless advertising is presented in a way the brain can absorb, it is simply not seen,” Raymond says.

So what does this mean for advertisers? A typical television advertisement consists of a series of attention-grabbing images interspersed with the product. But unless the scenes in the advertisement are cut to take account of attentional blinks, the brain is likely to ignore the information the advertiser wants to get across. The same applies to magazine advertisements, where viewers often register the main image but fail to pick up on the secondary images—the bits advertisers often desperately want us to see. Raymond says advertisers consistently fail to consider how easily the brain misses the point. It's not that they haven't realised that the space and time they have to get their message across has shrunk. But advertisers respond by cramming in ever more complex information. Raymond is opposed to this and her advice is simple: deliver your message in a straightforward manner and do so slowly, gently and concisely.

After her research on the attentional blink, she wondered whether attention would be linked to other processes in the brain, particularly emotion. Could our attentional state influence whether we like or dislike a brand, for example? Today, companies are hugely interested in the emotional value of their brands as they want their products to make us feel good. It is well known that if something elicits positive emotions then you are more likely to take notice of it. But Raymond's further research also demonstrates that if people are distracted by an image or a brand when performing an intellectually demanding task, they tend to instantly dislike the brands, regardless of their emotional value. So, for example, if you are reading a web page when a banner advertisement starts flashing, or are watching a film with intrusive product placement, it is probable you will come to dislike the brand whatever it is.

This contradicts the more-exposure-the-better rule most of the industry follows, says Raymond, and means that advertising can backfire horribly. Advertisers tend to buy as much exposure for a product as they can—through television and radio commercials, billboards, whatever they think will attract their target audiences—but again Raymond has found that this doesn't necessarily work in their favour. Perhaps the most dangerous time, says Raymond, is the holiday season when advertisers are madly competing to grab people's attention. “Marketers don't realise that humans digest information like they do food. Once they are full, if they are shown any more food, they're disgusted,” she says.

questionGroups.bodyHtml:
Questions 1–7

Do the following statements agree with the information in Reading Passage 1?

In boxes 1–7 on your answer sheet, write:

  • TRUE if the statement agrees with the information
  • FALSE if the statement contradicts the information
  • NOT GIVEN if there is no information about this

1 Jane Raymond states that Chillz mineral water is packaged in a way that is unattractive to consumers.

2 Consumers are still exposed to more advertising through television commercials than through the medium of the Internet.

3 Jamie Rayner says that people are no longer influenced by traditional advertisements.

4 According to Jamie Rayner, the reason that most products are discontinued is that advertising fails to attract consumers.

5 Jane Raymond believes that commercials should be simpler in their content.

6 Advertisements showing unfamiliar brands affect a person's concentration more than ones with familiar brands.

7 Jane Raymond suggests that a product should be advertised in as many ways as possible.

Questions 8–13

Choose NO MORE THAN THREE WORDS from the passage for each answer.

8 What group of consumers were specifically targeted in Jamie Rayner's research?

9 What subject did Jane Raymond study before focusing on the behaviour of consumers?

10 According to the writer, what important aspect of an advertisement in print do many people fail to notice?

11 According to the writer, what do companies today want their products to have in order to make consumers feel positive about themselves?

12 What does Jane Raymond say will annoy someone watching a movie?

13 According to Jane Raymond, when do advertisers promote their products most fiercely?

passageNotes.label: 段落 1
passageNotes.text:
核心段落 1（对应🔶13-4 至🔶13-5）：广告行业存在 “越努力吸引注意力，大脑越忽略” 的矛盾现象。英国威尔士班戈大学消费心理学家简・雷蒙德（Jane Raymond）以 Chillz 矿泉水为例，指出其透明塑料瓶形似冰雕的设计，能吸引购物者主动拿起瓶子。雷蒙德的研究聚焦于影响消费者购买的细微因素，为大企业提供广告效果评估与优化建议，核心目标是解决 “如何吸引消费者注意力” 的问题。
核心段落 2（对应🔶13-6）：当今快节奏消费环境中，“注意力” 是稀缺资源。消费者在商场购物、上网、看电视时，清醒状态下每 15 秒就可能接触一条广告，且去年全球企业广告支出达 4010 亿美元（数据来自英国世界广告研究中心）。但大量失败产品表明，企业的广告策略大多效果不佳。
核心段落 3（对应🔶13-7）：英国消费者行为咨询公司 ID Magasin 的研究总监杰米・雷纳（Jamie Rayner）提出，90% 的新产品早早夭折，根源是传统广告已失效。其团队针对消费者（尤其经常通勤者）展开研究，通过受试者佩戴的嵌入式摄像头眼镜记录广告注视情况，发现仅约 1% 的广告能被无提示回忆，多数广告未留下任何印象，即人们虽频繁看到广告，却未真正接收信息。
核心段落 4（对应🔶13-8）：雷蒙德解释了传统广告失效的原因。20 世纪 90 年代初，她从视觉处理研究转向消费心理学时，发现 “注意力眨眼” 现象：让受试者在屏幕字母数字流中寻找 “X”，若 “X” 与白色字母间隔半秒内出现，受试者便无法察觉。她指出，当某事物吸引注意力后，大脑短时间内会对其他事物 “视而不见”，而多数广告失效正是因人们处于严重注意力过载状态，广告未以大脑可吸收的方式呈现。
核心段落 5（对应🔶13-9）：针对广告商，雷蒙德提出建议：电视广告若未考虑 “注意力眨眼” 而随意切换画面，大脑会忽略核心信息；杂志广告中，读者常注意主画面却遗漏广告商重视的次要画面。广告商虽知晓传递信息的时空缩短，却反而塞入更多复杂信息，雷蒙德反对这种做法，主张广告应直接、缓慢、温和且简洁地传递信息。
核心段落 6（对应🔶13-10 至🔶13-11）：雷蒙德进一步研究发现，注意力与情感存在关联。企业重视品牌情感价值以让消费者产生好感，且能引发积极情感的事物更易被关注，但人们在完成需智力投入的任务时被广告干扰，会立刻厌恶该品牌（如网页弹窗广告、电影硬性植入）。这与行业 “曝光越多越好” 的规则相悖，广告可能适得其反，尤其节假日广告商激烈竞争时，过度曝光会让消费者像 “吃饱后再看到食物” 般反感。

items.text:
（1）题目 1：Jane Raymond states that Chillz mineral water is packaged in a way that is unattractive to consumers.
题目翻译：简・雷蒙德表示，Chillz 矿泉水的包装设计对消费者没有吸引力。
答案：FALSE（错误）
解析：定位🔶13-5 中 “Despite being made of clear plastic, it looks as if it has been carved from ice. This simple feature means shoppers are drawn to this bottle over the others on the shelf”，雷蒙德明确指出该矿泉水瓶的 “冰雕般外观” 能吸引购物者，与题干 “没有吸引力” 的描述矛盾，因此判定为 FALSE。

（2）题目 2：Consumers are still exposed to more advertising through television commercials than through the medium of the Internet.
题目翻译：消费者通过电视广告接触到的广告数量，仍多于通过互联网接触到的。
答案：NOT GIVEN（未提及）
解析：定位🔶13-6 中 “Whether we are taking our time shopping in a mall, surfing the Internet for information, or just watching television... consumers are surrounded by messages”，文中仅提及消费者在上网、看电视时均会接触广告，但未对比两者的广告数量多少，信息缺失，因此判定为 NOT GIVEN。

（3）题目 3：Jamie Rayner says that people are no longer influenced by traditional advertisements.
题目翻译：杰米・雷纳表示，人们不再受传统广告的影响。
答案：TRUE（正确）
解析：定位🔶13-7 中 “Nine out of ten new products meet an early death... the reason... is simple: conventional advertising has ceased to work”，“ceased to work” 意为 “失效”，即传统广告无法再影响消费者，导致产品失败，与题干描述一致，因此判定为 TRUE。

（4）题目 4：According to Jamie Rayner, the reason that most products are discontinued is that advertising fails to attract consumers.
题目翻译：根据杰米・雷纳的说法，多数产品停产的原因是广告未能吸引消费者。
答案：TRUE（正确）
解析：定位🔶13-7 中 “Nine out of ten new products meet an early death... the reason... is simple: conventional advertising has ceased to work”，雷纳将 “多数产品夭折（即停产）” 直接归因于 “传统广告失效”，而广告失效的核心是无法吸引消费者，与题干描述一致，因此判定为 TRUE。

（5）题目 5：Jane Raymond believes that commercials should be simpler in their content.
题目翻译：简・雷蒙德认为，广告内容应更简洁。
答案：TRUE（正确）
解析：定位🔶13-9 中 “Raymond is opposed to this and her advice is simple: deliver your message in a straightforward manner and do so slowly, gently and concisely”，“straightforward”“concisely” 均体现 “内容简洁” 的要求，说明雷蒙德主张广告内容更简单，与题干描述一致，因此判定为 TRUE。

（6）题目 6：Advertisements showing unfamiliar brands affect a person’s concentration more than ones with familiar brands.
题目翻译：陌生品牌的广告比熟悉品牌的广告更影响人的注意力。
答案：NOT GIVEN（未提及）
解析：定位🔶13-10 中 “if people are distracted by an image or a brand when performing an intellectually demanding task, they tend to instantly dislike the brands, regardless of their emotional value”，文中仅提到 “被品牌干扰时会厌恶该品牌”，但未区分 “陌生品牌” 与 “熟悉品牌” 对注意力的影响差异，信息缺失，因此判定为 NOT GIVEN。

（7）题目 7：Jane Raymond suggests that a product should be advertised in as many ways as possible.
题目翻译：简・雷蒙德建议，应通过尽可能多的方式为产品投放广告。
答案：FALSE（错误）
解析：定位🔶13-11 中 “This contradicts the more-exposure-the-better rule most of the industry follows, says Raymond... Advertisers tend to buy as much exposure ... but Raymond has found that this doesn't necessarily work”，雷蒙德明确反对 “曝光越多越好” 的原则，即不建议通过 “尽可能多的方式” 投放广告，与题干描述矛盾，因此判定为 FALSE。

questionExplanations.sectionTitle: 2. 填空题（Questions 8–13：NO MORE THAN THREE WORDS）

items.text:
（1）题目 8：What group of consumers were specifically targeted in Jamie Rayner’s research?
题目翻译：杰米・雷纳的研究中，专门针对的消费者群体是什么？
答案：regular commuters（经常通勤者）
解析：定位🔶13-7 中 “Rayner and his colleagues have measured how consumers—particularly regular commuters—react to advertising”，明确指出研究 “特别针对经常通勤者”，直接提取答案 “regular commuters”。

（2）题目 9：What subject did Jane Raymond study before focusing on the behaviour of consumers?
题目翻译：简・雷蒙德在专注于消费者行为研究之前，研究的学科是什么？
答案：visual processing（视觉处理）
解析：定位🔶13-8 中 “Her move from research in visual processing into consumer psychology began in the early 1990s”，可知雷蒙德在转向消费者行为研究前，专注于 “视觉处理”，因此答案为 “visual processing”。

（3）题目 10：According to the writer, what important aspect of an advertisement in print do many people fail to notice?
题目翻译：根据作者的说法，许多人会忽略印刷广告中的哪个重要部分？
答案：secondary images（次要画面）
解析：定位🔶13-9 中 “the same applies to magazine advertisements, where viewers often register the main image but fail to pick up on the secondary images—the bits advertisers often desperately want us to see”，“杂志广告” 属于 “印刷广告”，文中明确提到读者常忽略 “次要画面”，因此答案为 “secondary images”。

（4）题目 11：According to the writer, what do companies today want their products to have in order to make consumers feel positive about themselves?
题目翻译：根据作者的说法，如今企业希望其产品具备什么（特质），以让消费者产生积极感受？
答案：emotional value（情感价值）
解析：定位🔶13-10 中 “Today, companies are hugely interested in the emotional value of their brands as they want their products to make us feel good”，可知企业希望产品具有 “情感价值”，从而让消费者产生积极感受，因此答案为 “emotional value”。

（5）题目 12：What does Jane Raymond say will annoy someone watching a movie?
题目翻译：简・雷蒙德表示，什么会让看电影的人感到厌烦？
答案：intrusive product placement（硬性产品植入）
解析：定位🔶13-10 中 “watching a film with intrusive product placement, it is probable you will come to dislike the brand whatever it is”，可知 “电影中的硬性产品植入” 会让观众反感、厌烦，因此答案为 “intrusive product placement”。

（6）题目 13：According to Jane Raymond, when do advertisers promote their products most fiercely?
题目翻译：根据简・雷蒙德的说法，广告商在何时最激烈地推广产品？
答案：holiday season（节假日期间）
解析：定位🔶13-11 中 “Perhaps the most dangerous time, says Raymond, is the holiday season when advertisers are madly competing to grab people’s attention”，“madly competing” 体现 “推广最激烈”，对应的时间是 “节假日期间”，因此答案为 “holiday season”。

题目翻译：简・雷蒙德表示，什么会让看电影的人感到厌烦？
答案：intrusive product placement（硬性产品植入）
解析：定位🔶13-10 中 “watching a film with intrusive product placement, it is probable you will come to dislike the brand whatever it is”，可知 “电影中的硬性产品植入” 会让观众反感、厌烦，因此答案为 “intrusive product placement”。
题目翻译：根据简・雷蒙德的说法，广告商在何时最激烈地推广产品？
答案：holiday season（节假日期间）
解析：定位🔶13-11 中 “Perhaps the most dangerous time, says Raymond, is the holiday season when advertisers are madly competing to grab people’s attention”，“madly competing” 体现 “推广最激烈”，对应的时间是 “节假日期间”，因此答案为 “holiday season”。
